name: Protons
kicker: Positive particles in every nucleus · Their count sets the element
briefing: Protons are the positively charged particles packed into the nucleus of every atom, and the number of them decides which element an atom is: one for hydrogen, six for carbon, 79 for gold. Each proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron and is built from three smaller particles called quarks. Ernest Rutherford named the particle in 1920, from the Greek word for “first.”
answerHtml: protons (accept hydrogen nuclei or hydrogen ions; prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrons”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A “radius puzzle” about this particle began in 2010, when experiments using hydrogen atoms with a muon in place of the electron found this particle smaller than expected. This particle is made of two up quarks and one down quark.
tossups.r: The strong force holds these particles together in nuclei despite their electric repulsion. For 10 points, name this positively charged particle found in the nucleus of every atom.

tossups.p: Only about one percent of this particle’s mass comes from the masses of its quarks. This particle has a mass of about one atomic mass unit, and its charge, about 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs, is the same size as an electron’s.
tossups.r: Gluons hold its three quarks together. For 10 points, name this positive particle found in atomic nuclei along with neutrons.

tossups.p: In the late 1960s, electrons fired at this particle at the Stanford Linear Accelerator bounced off as if it held tiny, hard bits inside, which Richard Feynman called “partons.” Jerome Friedman, Henry Kendall, and Richard Taylor shared the 1990 Nobel Prize for those experiments.
tossups.r: Those bits turned out to be quarks. For 10 points, name this positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1955, Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain used the Bevatron at Berkeley to create the negatively charged antiparticle of this particle, winning the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. This particle is about 1,836 times as heavy as an electron.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this positively charged particle whose number in an atom’s nucleus gives the atomic number.

tossups.p: Some grand unified theories predict that this particle decays, but underground water tanks like Japan’s Super-Kamiokande have never seen it happen, showing that its lifetime is far longer than the age of the universe. A free neutron decays within minutes, but a free one of these particles is stable.
tossups.r: The simplest atom, hydrogen, has just one of these particles in its nucleus. For 10 points, name these positively charged nuclear particles.

tossups.p: Around 1917, Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles into nitrogen gas and detected these particles being knocked out, often called the first artificial change of one element into another. In 1920 he named these particles after the Greek word for “first.”
tossups.r: Each one carries a charge equal and opposite to an electron’s. For 10 points, name these positive particles in every atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1886, Eugen Goldstein found “canal rays” streaming backward through holes in the negative electrode of a gas-filled tube; in hydrogen gas, the lightest of those rays turned out to be these particles. Wilhelm Wien [“VEEN”] measured their charge-to-mass ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positively charged particles that join neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

tossups.p: Cancer treatments using beams of this particle can target tumors deep in the body because the particles release most of their energy at one depth, called the Bragg peak, and then stop. MRI machines make pictures by tracking the magnetic spins of these particles in the body’s hydrogen atoms.
tossups.r: Henry Moseley showed that the periodic table should be ordered by the number of these particles in each atom. For 10 points, name these positive nuclear particles.

tossups.p: In water, a lone one of these particles never stays free for long; it quickly attaches to a water molecule to form the hydronium ion. Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry defined acids as substances that give away these particles.
tossups.r: Bases accept them. For 10 points, name these positively charged particles found in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: The Large Hadron Collider near Geneva smashes together beams of these particles in a ring about 27 kilometers around, and its collisions led to the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson. These particles are baryons, made of three quarks each.
tossups.r: Each has a charge of plus one. For 10 points, name these particles that, together with neutrons, make up atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: About nine out of ten cosmic-ray particles striking Earth’s atmosphere from space are these particles, which also make up much of the solar wind. In the Sun’s core, energy production begins when two of these particles fuse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positive particles whose number in a nucleus is an element’s atomic number.

tossups.p: In positron emission, one of these particles inside a nucleus changes into a neutron, giving off a positron and a neutrino. In electron capture, one of these particles absorbs an inner electron and also becomes a neutron.
tossups.r: In beta-minus decay, a neutron turns into one of these. For 10 points, name these positive particles in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: In 1932, John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton used a high-voltage machine to fire these particles at lithium, splitting lithium nuclei into pairs of alpha particles. That same year, James Chadwick discovered the neutral particle that shares the nucleus with these particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positively charged nuclear particles, made of two up quarks and a down quark.

tossups.p: Peter Mitchell won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing that cells make ATP by letting these particles flow back across a membrane through the enzyme ATP synthase. In photosynthesis, these particles pile up inside thylakoids before rushing out through that enzyme.
tossups.r: Acids give them away. For 10 points, name these positive particles found in every atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: This particle is slightly lighter than the neutron. An atom’s mass number is found by adding the number of these particles to the number of neutrons, and in a neutral atom, the number of these particles equals the number of electrons.
tossups.r: Isotopes of an element all have the same number of these particles but different numbers of neutrons. For 10 points, name these positive nuclear particles.

trap.title: Which nuclear particle?
trap.body: Tossups about the atom have several look-alike answers. Neutrons sit in the nucleus too but have no charge, electrons orbit outside it with a negative charge, and quarks are the smaller pieces that make up both protons and neutrons. A clue about atomic number, positive charge, or acids giving something away points to this particle, while a neutral particle that James Chadwick found in 1932 is the neutron.
trap.fix: Positive charge, atomic number, the simplest nucleus, or two up quarks and a down quark mean this particle. No charge, Chadwick, or chain reactions mean the neutron; negative charge, J. J. Thomson, or orbitals mean the electron; and saying “nucleon” or “baryon” only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: protons (accept hydrogen nuclei or hydrogen ions; prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrons”)
